title: Does Matched-Pair Data Reduce Over-Defense in a Small Prompt-Injection Guard? A Controlled English–Indonesian Ablation
content: Small prompt-injection guards trained to catch attacks often over-defend, blocking ordinary customer messages that merely resemble attacks. Adding benign examples is a common remedy, but it is unclear whether writing each benign message as a matched companion of an attack helps beyond the added volume. We study this with a controlled ablation on a 0.8B guard that predicts injection and knowledge-base (KB) coverage in English and three Indonesian registers. Three conditions add 640 rows to the same 1,104-row base, with an unchanged base as control: no additions (D0), 320 matched attack–benign pairs (A), 640 benign messages with no attack companion (B), and A’s attacks with 320 unpaired benign messages (C). Each is trained with five seeds and scored on a 2,740-message adaptive development set and a separate 1,000-message audit. Adding benign data lowers benign false positives from 14.09% to 3.74% (A) on development and from 9.68% to 0.24% on the audit, with little change in mean recall. Benign-only data (B) lowers false positives further but loses 11–14 points of attack recall and reduces encoded-attack recall to 39–50%. The matched pairs are not reliably better than unpaired benign data: A is 1.43 points lower than C on development (seed-level p = 0.103) and no difference is resolved on the audit, with a descriptive gap in encoded messages (10.3% vs. 16.7%). The registered decision rule is therefore not met. Generation and review use the same model, authorship of the base data is mixed, and development was used adaptively; the results support the tested data additions but do not isolate a benefit of matched construction under these conditions.
